I've farmed this same 3.5 mu for 45 years, and I'm 69 now. My legs aren't as strong as they used to be, and my back aches when the weather turns. I never went to school — can't read a single word — but I know every inch of this land like the back of my hand. There's just me and my old woman at home. Our son works in Shijiazhuang and sends money when he can, but we don't count on it. We need the farm to feed ourselves and have a little cash left for medicine and the electric bill.

I plant all 3.5 mu to wheat and maize, the same double-crop I've always done. Can't afford to leave land idle, and we need both crops to get through the year.

For the wheat, I plant around October 8th or so, when the soil still has some warmth in it. I buy seed from Lao Zhang's shop in the village — it's a local improved variety, costs about 45 yuan per mu. I don't save my own wheat seed anymore; after two years it grows thin and weak. For fertilizer, I buy two big bags of compound fertilizer and one bag of urea for the whole 3.5 mu. That's what I've used for years. I spread the compound fertilizer in the furrows when I plant, and then in March or April, around Qingming, if the wheat looks a bit yellow, I broadcast the urea. Last year fertilizer jumped up 30 yuan a bag, so I only used half a bag of urea on the wheat instead of a full one. The yield was a bit lower, but I still had enough to eat. This year prices are still high, so I'll do the same: two bags of compound fertilizer and half to one bag of urea. I can't afford what the young people at the agricultural station recommend — they talk about 20 kilos per mu, but I don't have that kind of money. I think in bags, not kilos.

I irrigate the wheat twice. First time is in late winter or early spring, when the wheat is waking up. Second time is when the wheat is jointing — that's the important one. I used to irrigate three times, but the electric pump costs too much now. Two times is enough if the spring rain isn't too bad. My neighbor Old Wang only irrigates once and his wheat does okay, so two is fine for me. Every time I turn on that pump, the meter spins and my heart hurts.

For the maize, there's no rest after wheat harvest — usually around June 10th to 15th. As soon as the combine finishes the wheat, I get the corn in the ground. Sometimes the same day, sometimes the next morning. If you wait two days, you lose yield. I buy hybrid corn seed every year — can't save hybrid seed, it doesn't work. That's about 55 yuan per mu. For fertilizer, I put about one and a half bags of compound fertilizer and one bag of urea, all at planting. I dig a little hole, put in the fertilizer, drop the seed, cover it. At my age I can't do the fancy side-dressing some folks do — I put it all down at once and hope for rain. If the corn looks really hungry at knee-high and I have a bit of cash left, I might scatter a little more urea, but usually once is enough.

The corn gets watered once, maybe twice if it's very dry. Usually once at the big trumpet stage, around late July or early August. The last few years we've been lucky with summer rain, so once is usually enough. I pray for rain because pumping costs money.

I don't hire labor — can't afford it. My wife helps me spread fertilizer and pick out stones. I do the planting, irrigation, and spraying myself. Harvesting, I hire the combine — 50 yuan per mu for wheat, 60 for corn. That's the one thing I pay for because at my age I can't swing a sickle like I used to, and we don't own a machine.

I spray herbicide once on each crop. For the wheat, I do it in early spring when the weeds are small. For the corn, I spray about 10 days after the seedlings come up. If I see armyworms or borers in the corn — last year they were bad in the east corner — I buy a bottle of insecticide from the village shop and spray at night.

I expect about 800 jin per mu for the wheat, which is about 400 kg, and maybe 900 jin per mu for the corn, about 450 kg. Last year the wheat was only about 700 jin because the spring was dry, but the corn did alright. I'm not greedy. At 69, I just need enough to fill our bellies and pay the electric bill. I don't try new varieties or new methods — change is for young people with money to lose. I do what I've always done, a little less when money is tight, and it gets me through.
